01.note: Rava praised his student Rav Sehora to Rav Nahman as a great man, and Rav Nahman asked to meet him. When Rav Sehora needed a vow released, he came before Rav Nahman. Each time Rav Nahman suggested a circumstance the vow might not have anticipated, Rav Sehora answered that he had it in mind. Rav Nahman grew upset and told him to go away. Rav Sehora then reasoned, using Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's teaching that one should choose a path that wins honor from others, that he would never have vowed had he known it would upset Rav Nahman, and on that basis released the vow himself.
01.why: The Gemara has just stated Rav Nahman's ruling that a vow may be dissolved by finding grounds for regret; this story shows the search for such an opening, and the first of several cases where the trouble caused by the search itself becomes the opening.

02.note: Rabbi Shimon, son of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, came to the Sages to have a vow dissolved. Every time they suggested a circumstance he might not have considered, he said he had it in mind, and the Sages were troubled for so long that they moved from sun to shade and from shade back to sun. Then Botnit, son of Abba Shaul ben Botnit, asked him whether he would have vowed knowing the Sages would be troubled this way. He said no, and they dissolved the vow.
02.why: It follows the story of Rav Sehora as a second case in which the very difficulty of finding an opening to dissolve a vow becomes the opening.

03.note: Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosei came to the Sages to have a vow dissolved, and each time they suggested a circumstance he might not have considered, he said he had it in mind. A certain launderer, seeing the Sages troubled, hit him with a launderer's tool. Rabbi Yishmael said he would not have vowed had he known a launderer would hit him, and dissolved the vow.
03.why: It is another case where the trouble caused by a hard-to-dissolve vow becomes its opening. Rav Aha of Difti then objects that being hit was a new situation, which cannot be used as an opening; Ravina answers that heretics who trouble the Sages are common.

04.note: Abaye's wife had a daughter. Abaye wanted her to marry one of his relatives; his wife wanted one of hers. Abaye vowed that his wife could not benefit from him if she defied him and married the girl to her relative. She went and did so. Abaye came before Rav Yosef, who asked whether he would have vowed had he known she would defy him. Abaye said no, and Rav Yosef dissolved the vow.
04.why: The Gemara is collecting cases on finding grounds to dissolve vows. It then asks whether a vow can be dissolved on this kind of opening, and answers yes, citing a similar case decided by Rabbi Yosei.

05.note: A man vowed that his wife could not benefit from him if she went up to Jerusalem for the pilgrimage Festival. She defied him and went. He came before Rabbi Yosei, who asked whether he would have vowed had he known she would defy him. He said no, and Rabbi Yosei dissolved the vow.
05.why: The Gemara has just told how Rav Yosef dissolved Abaye's vow on the ground that he never expected his wife to defy him, and asks whether such an opening is valid. This earlier case is cited from the Tosefta as proof that it is.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who dissolved the man's vow

One of the three festivals (Passover, Shavuot, Sukkot) when Jews went up to the Temple in Jerusalem.

06.note: A man claimed money from another before Rava. The borrower said he had already repaid, and Rava told him to take an oath that he had. The borrower hid the money inside a hollow cane, leaned on it on his way to court, and asked the lender to hold the cane while he took the Torah scroll. He swore that he had repaid everything that had been in his possession. The angry lender broke the cane, the coins fell to the ground, and it turned out the oath was technically true.
06.why: The Gemara is asking why a court warns a person that his oath is taken by the court's understanding and not his own. It answers that the warning is meant to rule out tricks like this cane.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who heard the case and ordered the borrower to swear

terms.meaning: In a money dispute, a court could require one party to swear while holding a Torah scroll that his claim was true.
Courts warned a person that his oath counts by its plain meaning as the court understands it, not by any private intention.

07.note: A man in a court dispute deposited his documents supporting his claim with the court and said: if I do not come back within thirty days, these documents are void. He was prevented by circumstances beyond his control and did not come. Rav Huna ruled the documents void. Rava disagreed: the man was a victim of circumstances, and the Torah exempts such a person, as in the verse about the young woman who was raped: to her you shall do nothing.
07.why: The Mishna has just said that vows blocked by circumstances beyond one's control, like illness or a river, are not binding. The Gemara brings this case to ask whether the same applies to a condition a man set on himself, and then tests Rava's view against other rulings.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who ruled the man's documents void

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who argued that the man, prevented by circumstances, was exempt

terms.meaning: In the Sages' language, being 'forced' (anus): something outside a person's power that stopped him from doing what he undertook.

08.note: A man gave agents a bill of divorce for his wife and said: if I do not return within thirty days, let this be a divorce. He came back on the thirtieth day, but the ferry was on the other side of the river and he could not cross. He called out to the people across the river: See that I have arrived! Shmuel ruled that this does not count as arriving.
08.why: The Gemara is challenging Rava's view that a person prevented by circumstances is exempt: here the man was prevented too, yet Shmuel let the divorce take effect. It answers that a ferry is a foreseeable obstacle he should have stipulated for.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ruled that the man had not arrived in time

terms.meaning: A get: the document a husband gives his wife to end the marriage. It can be made to take effect on a condition.
A boat that carried people across the river; the text says it was on the far side.

09.note: A middleman took a donkey to sell but could not find a buyer. On his way back to the owner, the donkey met with an accident, and Rav Nahman ordered the middleman to pay. Rava objected from a teaching that someone carrying goods is liable for an accident on the way there but exempt on the way back. Rav Nahman answered that a middleman's return trip counts as the way there, since if he found a buyer even at the owner's door, he would still sell.
09.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that a man taking goods to show his father-in-law is liable like a borrower on the way there but only like a paid guardian on the way back; this case shows the rule does not apply to a middleman.

terms.meaning: An agent who takes another person's goods to sell on his behalf.
A borrower must pay even for unavoidable loss; a paid guardian of goods is exempt for such loss.

10.note: Rav Helbo fell ill and no one came to visit him. Rav Kahana reminded the Sages of a student of Rabbi Akiva who fell ill and whom the Sages did not visit. Rabbi Akiva visited, and because the floor was swept and sprinkled with water before the student, he recovered. The student said: My teacher, you revived me. Rabbi Akiva went out and taught that anyone who does not visit the sick is as if he spills blood.
10.why: The discussion is about the duty of visiting the sick: what it means that it has no fixed measure, and how a visitor eases suffering. This story shows that neglecting the duty can cost a life.

11.note: Rav Yosef fell ill and forgot what he had learned. His student Abaye restored his learning by reviewing it before him. The Gemara says this is the background to the many places in the Talmud where Rav Yosef says he never heard a teaching, and Abaye answers: you told it to us yourself, from this source.
11.why: Rav Yosef has just explained a verse to mean that a sick person forgets his studies; this story shows it happening to him.

12.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi learned thirteen versions of a teaching and taught seven of them to Rabbi Hiyya. Later he fell ill and forgot them. Rabbi Hiyya restored the seven he had been taught, but six were lost. A launderer had overheard Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi studying them, so Rabbi Hiyya learned them from the launderer and restored them too. When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw the launderer, he said: You made me and Hiyya. Some say he said: You made Hiyya, and Hiyya made me.
12.why: It follows the story of Rav Yosef as a second case of a sick Sage forgetting his learning, illustrating the teaching that a sick person forgets his studies.

13.note: People told Rabba bar Sheila that a man had died. He was tall and was riding a small mule; when he reached a bridge the mule took fright and threw him, and although he had not far to fall, he died. Rabba bar Sheila applied the verse to him: They stand this day according to Your judgments.
13.why: Rav has just taught from this verse that when a person's time has come, everything becomes God's agent to kill him; the story shows a death from a fall that should have been harmless.

people.name: Rabba bar Sheila
people.about: A Sage who heard of the man's death and applied a verse to it

14.note: Shmuel saw a frog carrying a scorpion across a river. On the other side the scorpion stung a man, and he died. Shmuel applied the verse to him: They stand this day according to Your judgments.
14.why: Rav has just taught from this verse that when a person's time has come, all creatures become God's agents to kill him; here even a frog and a scorpion serve that purpose.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who saw the frog and scorpion and applied a verse to the death

15.note: A man had a son who stole sheaves of flax, and the father vowed that the son could not benefit from his property. People asked him: what if your grandson becomes a Torah scholar? He said: let this son of mine acquire the property, and if my grandson becomes a Torah scholar, let him acquire it. The question was then asked what the ruling is; the text of the story does not give the answer.
15.why: The Gemara is discussing gifts made only to get around a vow. The Sages of Pumbedita, Rav Nahman and Rav Ashi then debate whether the son can acquire the property just to pass it on to his son.

terms.meaning: A person devoted to study of the Torah and its law.
A vow barring someone from gaining anything from the vower's property.

16.note: Rabbi Yirmeya fell ill, and a doctor came to heal him. The doctor saw a gourd in the house, turned around and left, saying: This man has an angel of death in his house, and I should go in to heal him?
16.why: A teaching has just said that gourds are what the sick eat with their bread; the Gemara cites this story as a challenge, since the doctor treated a gourd as deadly for the sick. It then answers that soft and hard gourds, or the gourd and its innards, differ.

17.note: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda were eating porridge together, one with his fingers and the other with a fork. The one with the fork said: How long will you feed me your filth? The one with his fingers answered: How long will you feed me your spittle?
17.why: The Gemara has been collecting sayings about porridge, including Rav's view that porridge tastes best eaten with the fingers; this exchange between two Sages over the same habit follows.

18.note: Figs called belospayin were brought before Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yehuda ate, but Rabbi Shimon did not. Rabbi Yehuda asked why, and Rabbi Shimon said these figs never leave the intestines. Rabbi Yehuda replied: all the more reason to rely on them to keep us full tomorrow.
18.why: It belongs to a run of short anecdotes about food and eating that the Gemara strings together in its discussion of what counts as cooked food.

19.note: Rabbi Yehuda was sitting before Rabbi Tarfon, who told him his face looked ruddy that day. Rabbi Yehuda explained that the night before, the students had gone out to the field, were brought beets, and ate them without salt; had they eaten them with salt, their faces would have been ruddier still.
19.why: It is one of a chain of anecdotes about food and about Rabbi Yehuda, the next several of which explain his ruddy face.

20.note: A certain noblewoman said to Rabbi Yehuda, whose face was ruddy: How can a teacher be a drunk? He answered that she could stake his credibility on it: he tasted wine only for kiddush, havdala and the four cups of Passover, and after those he bound his temples from Passover to Shavuot. His face shone, he said, because of the verse: A man's wisdom makes his face to shine.
20.why: It continues a chain of anecdotes about Rabbi Yehuda's ruddy face; another explanation follows, given to a heretic.
